title: Construct the Minimum Bitwise Array I
statement: You get an array `nums` of `n` prime numbers. Return an array `ans` of the same length in which `ans[i]` is the smallest non-negative integer whose bitwise OR with the next integer, `ans[i] | (ans[i] + 1)`, equals `nums[i]`. Each index is solved on its own, and when no integer has this property for `nums[i]`, `ans[i]` is `-1`.
constraints: Every nums[i] is a prime number
notes:
## Intuition

Adding 1 to `x` turns its trailing 1 bits into 0s and its lowest 0 bit into a 1. OR-ing that with `x` brings the trailing 1s back, so `x | (x + 1)` is simply `x` with its lowest 0 bit switched on. Two facts follow:

- The result is always odd, so the only even prime, 2, has no answer.
- If an odd `num` ends in a run of `t` ones, clearing any one bit of that run gives a valid `x` (that bit becomes the lowest 0 of `x`). Clearing the highest bit of the run, worth `2^(t - 1)`, removes the most, so it gives the smallest `x`.

Trying every `x` from 0 to `num` also works with these small limits, but the bit trick answers each number in constant time.

## Approach

1. For each `num`, if it is even (that is, 2), push `-1`.
2. Otherwise compute `lowestZero = (num + 1) & ~num`: the carry from adding 1 runs through the trailing ones and stops on the lowest 0 bit, and `& ~num` keeps only that bit.
3. `lowestZero >> 1` is the highest bit of the trailing run of ones; push `num` minus it.
4. Return `ans`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [2, 3, 5, 7]`. `2` is even, so push `-1`. `3` is `11`: `lowestZero = 4`, half of it is 2, push `1`. `5` is `101`: `lowestZero = 6 & ~5 = 2`, half is 1, push `4`. `7` is `111`: `lowestZero = 8`, half is 4, push `3`. The result is `[-1, 1, 4, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): a few bit operations per number.
- Space: O(1) besides the output `ans`.

## Pitfalls

- `num - 1` is always valid for an odd `num`, but not always the smallest: for 7 it gives 6, while 3 also works.
- Only bits inside the trailing run of ones may be cleared: for 13 (`1101`) the answer is 12, not 9, because `9 | 10 = 11`.
- Do not forget 2: no `x` reaches an even number.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ans` | the answers found so far, one per prime |
| `num` | the prime being solved |
| `lowestZero` | the value of the lowest 0 bit of `num` |

narration.3: Each prime is solved on its own.
narration.4: x | (x + 1) is always odd, so an even target (only 2) is unreachable.
narration.5: No x works for 2, so record -1.
narration.7: The carry from num + 1 stops on the lowest 0 bit; & ~num keeps just that bit.
narration.8: Half of it is the top bit of the trailing 1s; clearing that bit gives the smallest valid x.
narration.11: Every prime now has its answer.
